name: AI GridWatch data center project tracker
caveat:
A working set of identified proposals a community can track, not a census — most of the country's activity is not in here yet.

**Each row carries its own provenance.** Rows showing a verification date link to reporting or the governing body's own record and were read on that date; rows marked *unverified* have no source on record — a lead to check, not a fact to cite.

**Stage is derived, not asserted.** *Hearing scheduled*, *Awaiting decision*, *Approved* and *Withdrawn* are computed from each row's milestone dates on every rebuild, so a hearing date that has passed stops reading 'scheduled'. Hearings get moved and projects re-file under new names — treat a scheduled date as the earliest to act by, and confirm with the clerk before relying on it. Leads are mined into data/project_candidates.json and promoted here only after a human reads a primary source.

schema.name: Project or code name.
schema.filing_llc: Shell LLC on the filing (ties to the campus registry), or blank.
schema.locality: Town or county the project sits in.
schema.size_mw: Planned IT/critical load in MW, or blank.
schema.announced: ISO date first publicly proposed, or blank.
schema.rezoning_filed: ISO date the rezoning/permit application was filed, or blank.
schema.hearing_date: ISO date of the next/decisive public hearing, or blank.
schema.decided_date: ISO date a terminal decision was reached, or blank.
schema.outcome: approved | denied | withdrawn | blank (blank = still live).
schema.stage: DERIVED status shown on the page (Hearing scheduled, Awaiting decision, In review, Proposed, Rumored, Approved, Denied, Withdrawn).
schema.days_to_hearing: DERIVED days until the hearing (negative once past), or blank.
schema.source: Primary URL backing the current status.
schema.as_of: ISO date the source was read, or blank.
schema.verified: true if a source is on record.

projects.name: PW Digital Gateway
projects.note: Approved in 2023 (4-3-1) but the rezoning was judicially voided over defective hearing notice; county and developer dropped their appeals in 2026, ending the project as approved.

events.summary: Prince William Board of Supervisors approved the rezoning 4-3-1 after a ~27-hour public hearing - roughly 2,100 acres / 23M sq ft along Pageland Lane, billed as the world's largest data center corridor.
Virginia's Court of Appeals upheld a lower-court ruling voiding the rezoning over defective public-hearing notice (March 2026).
County dropped its legal appeals (~$1.7M spent defending the project) and the developer withdrew, terminating the approved Digital Gateway (April 2026).

projects.name: Plaza 500 (Lincolnia)
projects.note: By-right data center on the 34-acre 6299 Edsall Road site; the required substation faces a Fairfax County Planning Commission Public Facilities (2232) review on Sept 24, 2026 amid organized opposition.

events.summary: Dominion Energy filed its application with Virginia's State Corporation Commission for the Edsall transmission line connecting the future substation to the Van Dorn substation.
The Virginia State Corporation Commission issued its Final Order approving Dominion Energy's Edsall-to-Van Dorn transmission line project.

Starwood Capital filed permit applications and building plans for Plaza 500 South, the first of two data center buildings on the 34-acre 6299 Edsall Road site (by-right, no rezoning hearing required).
ALXnow reported that Alexandria officials and residents are pushing back against Starwood Capital Group's planned Plaza 500 data center at 6299 Edsall Road near the city line.
About 100 residents attended the Mason District Land Use Committee meeting on July 28 where Dominion Energy presented the proposed Edsall Road substation, and community members spoke out against it.
Rep. Don Beyer sent an official letter dated July 30 to the Fairfax County Planning Commission requesting denial of the 2232 permit application for Dominion's proposed Edsall Road substation.
In a letter dated Aug. 3, Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskins wrote on behalf of the City Council to ask the Fairfax County Planning Commission to deny the Edsall Data Center Substation 2232 application.
Rep. Don Beyer, Alexandria's mayor and city council, and residents pressed Fairfax County to deny the substation that would power the campus - proposed within ~100 ft of homes.
Mason District Supervisor Andres Jimenez called on the Fairfax County Planning Commission to reject the proposed Edsall Road substation serving the Plaza 500 data center.
The Mason District Land Use Committee is scheduled to decide whether to recommend the Edsall Road substation to the Planning Commission at 7:30 p.m. on Sept. 22.
Fairfax County Planning Commission Public Facilities (2232) review of the Edsall Road substation, 7 p.m. - the decisive vote residents can weigh in on.

projects.name: Project Iron Spur
projects.note: ~129-acre hyperscale campus proposed across from Rural Hall town hall; Forsyth County Planning Board recommended denial. Commissioners held the public hearing July 30, 2026 - decision pending.

events.summary: Charlotte-based developer Drox Group LLC presented its proposed hyperscale data center on roughly 129 acres in Rural Hall at a March community meeting, where residents raised concerns about noise, pollution, and energy and water demands.
The Rural Hall Town Council unanimously passed a resolution in April opposing the rezoning needed for the Drox Group data center.

The Forsyth County (City-County) Planning Board voted on Thursday, June 11 to recommend denying Drox Group's rezoning request for the $3 billion, 129-acre project, with staff citing potential significant offsite impacts to nearby residents.

The Rural Hall Town Council voted to withdraw its opposition and back the project after Mayor Terry Bennett said the developer made a written promise that, if the county approved rezoning, the town could annex the site and collect tax revenue; the resolution carries no legal weight in the county process.

Forsyth County Planning Board recommended denial, citing scale and intensity that 'could result in significant offsite impacts to nearby residents.' Rural Hall town officials reversed their opposition after a tax-revenue annexation offer.
County commissioners held the public hearing on the rezoning after months of resident opposition; a final decision was pending as of this record.

The Forsyth County Board of Commissioners voted 5-2 to deny the rezoning request for Project Iron Spur, with only Don Martin and Gloria Whisenhunt voting in support, following six months of review, over 400 emails, and dozens of public speakers.

projects.name: Meta Hyperion
projects.note: Approved and under construction - a ~5 GW, ~$27B campus. Louisiana approved new Entergy natural-gas generation to serve it; ratepayer cost allocation is the live fight, not the siting.

events.summary: Gov. Jeff Landry and Meta announced on December 4, 2024 that Meta will build a $10 billion AI data center on a 2,250-acre site in Richland Parish, described as Meta's largest data center, with construction continuing through 2030.

The Louisiana Public Service Commission approved Entergy Louisiana's application on August 20, 2025 to construct three new gas plants and related transmission to power Meta's Richland Parish data center, despite opposition.
Heavy construction equipment was documented at the Meta data center site in Holly Ridge, Louisiana on October 16, 2025.

Entergy Louisiana broke ground on December 1, 2025 on a pair of gas power plants at the Franklin Farms Power Station in Richland Parish to serve Meta's data center, with the complex expected operational in late 2028.

In December 2025 the PSC adopted a regulatory framework aligned with Gov. Landry's 'Lightning Speed Initiative' to expedite approvals for large industrial projects; tensions between commissioners surfaced at the meeting.
Campus scaled to ~5 GW and ~$27B (up from an announced $10B); Entergy's plan for ten new gas units to serve it advanced through the Louisiana PSC (early 2026).
Earthjustice filed a motion on January 14, 2026 requesting that the PSC investigate the Meta-Blue Owl financing deal's impact on ratepayer protections.
The Louisiana PSC declined on February 25, 2026 to investigate Meta's financing arrangement with Blue Owl Capital, alarming consumer and environmental groups.

The Louisiana PSC voted on April 15, 2026 to adopt a fast-track schedule for Entergy Louisiana's application to build seven additional gas plants for the Hyperion project, with a final decision scheduled for December 2026.

Meta announced in late July 2026 that it is expanding its Hyperion data center in Richland Parish to 5 gigawatts of compute capacity at a total cost of more than $50 billion, more than double the previous $27 billion budget.

The Louisiana PSC voted 3-1 on August 12, 2026 to reject an administrative law judge's recommendation, allowing Meta to avoid complying with subpoenas and keep Richland Parish data center details confidential.

projects.name: Burkhalter Road data center (4AM Development)
projects.note: Two-story 230,000 sq ft data center plus a 32,000 sq ft substation on ~26.5 acres at 6539 Burkhalter Road (R-4 residential to Office & Business rezoning). Planning Commission recommended approval 5-1; City Council decides Aug 18, 2026. Bulloch County, separately, has been extending data-center moratoriums.

events.summary: 4AM Development LLC, the applicant on the Burkhalter Road rezoning, was registered with the State of Georgia on December 15, 2023, with a principal office in Appling, Georgia and authorizing member Bobby Bagwell.

In January 2024, Four Guys Development LLC obtained city annexation of the roughly 26.94-acre Burkhalter Road parcel, then proposing a 'cottage court' subdivision of about 87 homes (later rezoned R-4).
On January 10, 2025, Habersham Development Group purchased the Burkhalter Road property for approximately $2.75 million.
On August 29, 2025, 4AM Development LLC acquired the roughly 27-acre Burkhalter Road parcel from Habersham Development Group in a zero-dollar transfer.
A February 2026 intergovernmental agreement between Statesboro and Bulloch County established the jointly funded Burkhalter Road / Highway 67 corridor improvement project.
On February 17, 2026, the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution imposing a 90-day moratorium on the permitting of data centers in unincorporated Bulloch County.

An economic impact study commissioned by the Development Authority of Bulloch County, dated May 2026, forecast the Burkhalter Road data center would draw $1.2 billion in total investment over 10 years while creating only 12 jobs with a $1.2 million annual payroll.
On May 5, 2026, the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners voted 5-0 to extend its data center moratorium through December 31, 2026, and voiced opposition to data centers in the unincorporated county.
On June 2, 2026, Statesboro City Council approved its Data Center Ordinance on second reading in a 3-1 vote, with Councilwoman Shari Barr opposing.

Statesboro Planning Commission voted 5-1 to recommend approval of 4AM Development LLC's rezoning of ~26.5 acres at 6539 Burkhalter Road (chair dissenting), with a condition dedicating a 10-ft frontage strip for future road work.

On August 4, 2026, Statesboro City Council (morning meeting) and the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners (evening meeting) each authorized negotiations with Kimley-Horn & Associates to design jointly funded Burkhalter Road corridor upgrades.

Dozens of Bulloch County residents gathered outside Statesboro City Hall on Saturday, August 8, 2026, carrying signs and chanting to oppose the proposed Burkhalter Road data center rezoning, citing noise, air pollution, water usage and wildlife concerns.
Statesboro City Council scheduled to consider the rezoning request - the decisive vote.

projects.name: West Erwin Street data center (Barrio Resources)
projects.note: Special use permit for a bitcoin-mining data center on ~1.92 acres near downtown (W. Erwin St & N. Ross Ave) denied 5-2 by the Planning & Zoning Commission - staff found it inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map and comprehensive plan, after resident opposition over water, noise, and proximity to homes. Applicant may appeal.

events.summary: Barrio Energy announced acquisition of a 12 MW data center property west of downtown Tyler, its fifth Texas site within ERCOT; president Ivan Pinney called Tyler 'an ideal location.'
A community meeting was announced for the proposed data center at 1101-1105 W. Erwin Street; the Planning & Zoning public hearing was set for July 7 at 1:30 p.m.

Vulcan Core and Barrio held a community input meeting on W. Erwin Street; developer Mark Buntsev claimed no negative effects on homes, projected $550,000/year in electricity taxes and 7-10 jobs; residents questioned water use, noise, and site selection.

Tyler Morning Telegraph reported project specs: eight 40-ft containers (four computing, four cooling), 12 MW capacity, MicroBT mining equipment, closed-loop cooling with no municipal water use, and an independent acoustic study claiming 35 dB at the nearest house vs. 45 dB ambient.

Tyler mayor-elect Stuart Hene, who won the runoff with 57% of the vote, said the data center proposal on West Erwin Street would face 'an uphill battle' after attending the developer's community meeting.

Tyler P&Z denied the special use permit 5-2. Planning staff: 'inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map and the Tyler Tomorrow Comprehensive Plan.' Residents cited water use, noise, and proximity to surrounding homes.

Tyler Morning Telegraph detailed the 3.5-hour hearing: 26 residents spoke against the project and 5 in favor (including 2 Vulcan Core representatives); planning director Kyle Kingma found the proposal inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map and comprehensive plan; Chairman David Hudson noted the applicant may appeal to City Council.

The Cooldown reported on the denial, quoting resident Hannah Morris: 'We were told that it's a close-knit system, but water doesn't magically appear'; noted residents anticipate the developer will appeal.

projects.name: Aligned Data Centers - Pataskala industrial park
projects.note: 200 MW campus in three buildings on ~89 acres at Broad St SW & Mink St SW. Planning & Zoning recommended rejection 5-2 after protests filled City Hall; City Council decides Aug 25, 2026 (5:30 p.m.). Council has separately advanced a ballot measure that could ban large data centers.

events.summary: Aligned Data Centers purchased three parcels totaling about 89.4 acres at 6770 Mink St. in Pataskala for $13.9 million (year reported as 2023).
Aligned filed its site plan application with the City of Pataskala to begin the review process for the three-building data center campus (reported as November 2025).
Pataskala Planning & Zoning Commission voted 5-2 to recommend that City Council reject Aligned's site plan, hours after residents rallied on the City Hall lawn.

Ohio Free Press reported that residents at the June 3 zoning meeting raised concerns the campus would use Bloom Energy fuel cells requiring roughly 15,000 decatherms of natural gas and cited noise from a comparable Aligned facility in Sandusky, Ohio.

Pataskala organizers reported a petition drive underway to put a charter amendment banning data centers with peak load over 25 megawatts on the ballot, needing at least 310 valid signatures (goal 500) and planning to submit them the week of July 6.

The Columbus Dispatch reported that Pataskala planning and zoning staff had recommended approval of Aligned's 200-megawatt plan, but the planning and zoning commission voted 5-2 to recommend rejection, sending the decision to City Council's Aug. 25 hearing.

Pataskala City Council passed an ordinance placing a charter amendment that could ban large data centers on the November ballot, expediting the vote to meet the Aug. 5 filing deadline for the Nov. 3 ballot.
Pataskala City Council public hearing on the site plan, 5:30 p.m., council chambers - the decisive vote.

projects.name: King of Prussia campus (MLP Ventures)
projects.note: Five-site, 4.6M sq ft campus across King of Prussia. Applications were filed in early March 2026, roughly ten days before Upper Merion's new data-center ordinance took effect - exempting them from its residential buffer, noise, and water-use rules. The township Planning Commission voted against three of the proposals in July 2026; review continues amid packed hearings and organized opposition.

events.summary: Applications filed in early March 2026, ~10 days before Upper Merion's new data-center ordinance took effect - grandfathering the projects out of its residential buffer, noise, and water-use requirements.
The 4.6M sq ft, five-site plan by MLP Ventures was publicly unveiled; neighbor pushback began immediately.
In July 2026 the Upper Merion Planning Commission voted against three of the data-center proposals; hundreds of residents packed hearings in opposition. Township review continues.

projects.name: AWS Calvert Technology Center
projects.note: Eight data center buildings (266,000-332,000 sq ft each) proposed at 1650 Calvert Cliffs Parkway on Constellation-owned parcels near the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant. AWS formally withdrew the concept site plan on Aug 4, 2026 - after first-round county review comments and before any resubmission. Timeline documented on the county's own project page.

events.summary: Amazon Data Services Inc. submitted initial site plan documents; the application was formally accepted for processing May 27, 2026.
County agencies completed first-round review of the concept site plan and returned comments to AWS.
AWS formally withdrew the Calvert Technology Center concept site plan application, per the county's project page, without resubmitting a revised plan.

projects.name: xAI Colossus
projects.note: Operating and expanding (~$20B, ~2 GW ambition). The live fight is air quality: on-site gas turbines in southwest Memphis - an area already failing federal ozone standards - drew a Clean Air Act suit. Environmental groups' tracking put unpermitted turbines at 27 in Feb 2026, growing to 59 by mid-2026 across the Colossus complex (incl. Colossus 2 in Southaven, MS).

events.summary: At the Greater Memphis Chamber's Annual Chairman's Luncheon, xAI announced an expansion of its Colossus supercomputer to a minimum of one million GPUs, described as the largest capital investment in the region's history.
The Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the NAACP, filed a 60-day notice of intent to sue xAI over at least 35 unpermitted combustion turbines at the Colossus data center near Memphis.
In July 2025, after SELC threatened a citizen suit, the Shelby County Health Department issued an air permit covering 15 of the 30+ turbines then operating unpermitted at the Memphis site.

After a seven-hour hearing at the University of Memphis attended by hundreds, the Memphis and Shelby County Air Pollution Control Board dismissed the appeal of xAI's air permit on grounds of mootness.

xAI announced a more than $20 billion investment in a Southaven, Mississippi data center (MACROHARDRR) that would bring its computing power to nearly 2 gigawatts; the Mississippi Development Authority approved xAI for its Data Center Incentive program.

Earthjustice and the Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, sent a 60-day notice of intent to sue xAI over 27 unpermitted gas turbines in Southaven powering the Colossus 2 data center.
xAI filed a permit for a $659.3 million, 75-foot, four-story building of roughly 312,000 square feet on a parcel adjacent to its Colossus 2 site on Tulane Road, reported March 3, 2026.

The Mississippi Environmental Quality Permit Board unanimously approved a PSD construction permit allowing xAI affiliate MZX Tech to install 41 permanent methane gas turbines at its Southaven plant powering the Memphis data center operations.
NAACP, represented by Earthjustice and SELC, filed a Clean Air Act suit against xAI and MZX Tech (N.D. Miss.) over unpermitted gas turbines serving the Colossus complex.

The NAACP asked the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi for a preliminary injunction to halt xAI's gas turbines at its Southaven facility while the Clean Air Act lawsuit proceeds, as reported May 6, 2026.

The U.S. Department of Justice moved to intervene in the NAACP's Clean Air Act suit and urged the court to dismiss it, arguing that shutting off xAI's Southaven turbines would harm national, economic and energy security because the Grok AI model supports Department of War military operations, including recent strikes involving Iran.

projects.name: Nordson campus data center (Cervenka)
projects.note: Use variance to convert three newer buildings on the longtime Nordson Corporation campus into a data center complex - denied by the Board of Zoning Appeals on July 30, 2026, less than 24 hours after a hearing where 100+ residents packed City Hall and spilled onto the lawn. The developer's remaining path is an appeal in Lorain County Common Pleas Court.

events.summary: Amherst Board of Zoning Appeals denied the use variance, releasing its decision less than 24 hours after a packed hearing (100+ residents, capacity limits pushed the crowd outside).

projects.name: Hexa Builders data center (Black Horse Pike)
projects.note: Previously-approved warehouse project at 3043 South Black Horse Pike amended in early April 2026 to include a 1,000,000 sq ft data center. Two weeks later the township council stripped data-center permissions from the site and banned data centers township-wide; the planning board then deemed the amended application incomplete. Hexa is now suing the township for $300M+. Not dead - the litigation decides it.

events.summary: Monroe Township Council adopted Resolution R:221-2019, declaring the Commercial Corridor Rehabilitation Area along Black Horse Pike (Block 8401, Lots 8, 9, and 10, approximately 158 acres) an area in need of redevelopment.

Monroe Township adopted Ordinance O:04-2023, approving the Hexa Builders Redevelopment Plan (revised November 15, 2022) permitting warehouse, storage, and distribution uses on the 158-acre site; data centers were not included as a permitted use.

The New Jersey Pinelands Commission published a public notice and scheduled a hearing on Monroe Township Ordinance O:04-2023 to determine whether the Hexa Builders Redevelopment Plan conformed with the Pinelands Comprehensive Management Plan.

Monroe Township Council adopted Ordinance O:02-2025, amending the Hexa Builders Redevelopment Plan to add data centers and associated infrastructure (electrical systems, cooling equipment, network infrastructure, emissions control) as a permitted use.

Residents within 200 feet of the Hexa Builders redevelopment site received certified mail notice of a January 8, 2026 planning board meeting regarding a 1.6-million-square-foot warehouse proposal at 3043 South Black Horse Pike.
At a January 8 Monroe Planning Board meeting, residents objected to the data center proposal, but the board approved Hexa's project that evening.
On January 28 the Monroe Township Council directed the planning board to develop stricter data center standards, citing resident opposition.
On February 2 the Monroe Planning Board memorialized its approval of Hexa's project in a written resolution.

More than 100 residents packed a Monroe Township Council meeting lasting five hours; environmental groups including CRAN, Sustain South Jersey, Pinelands Alliance, and Food and Water Watch attended and raised concerns about the data center's water, energy, and noise impacts.

Mayor Gregory Wolfe announced in a Facebook video that a data center would not be coming to Monroe Township and that the council would remove data centers as a permitted use from the Hexa Redevelopment Plan at the March 25 meeting.
At a March 25 council meeting, Monroe Township leaders heard resident concerns and approved a motion to change the ordinance so data centers could not be built in the community.

Council introduced Ordinance O:20-2026 to eliminate data center use from the Hexa Builders Redevelopment Plan; all council members except John Valentine voted to introduce it, with Valentine wanting a broader ban and better public notification instead.
Hexa Builders filed an amended application in early April 2026 converting one approved warehouse into a 1M sq ft data center at 3043 South Black Horse Pike.
The Monroe Township council and ordinance committee voted to introduce a separate township-wide data center ban ordinance, with a final adoption vote scheduled for April 22.
Township council passed two ordinances: one stripping data-center permissions from the specific site, the other banning data centers township-wide.
CBS Philadelphia reported on the ban, quoting Mayor Wolfe stating that Monroe Township has now banned any data center use from ever coming to the township.
Planning board unanimously deemed the amended site-plan application incomplete - blocking the project without rejecting it on the merits.

At the completeness review, township planner Christopher Dochney cited multiple application deficiencies including a missing environmental assessment, no Pinelands Certificate of Filing, unsigned plans, absent stormwater maintenance schedule, and incomplete electrical infrastructure documentation covering 3+ acres.
Monroe Township's data center ban officially took effect on May 13.

A coalition of 60 environmental, labor, and community organizations sent a letter to Governor Sherrill urging her to use emergency powers to impose a statewide moratorium on data centers consuming 20+ megawatts; Monroe Township resident Aleasha Whipple was quoted as a local organizer.
On May 22 Hexa presented its still-pending application, including the data center component, at a packed special planning board meeting attended by opposed residents.

On June 5 Hexa Builders filed a 104-page, 20-count lawsuit in New Jersey Superior Court alleging First and 14th Amendment and state-law violations and seeking $300 million after Monroe denied its application.
On July 6 the case was moved from New Jersey Superior Court to federal court in Camden; the Superior Court case closed.
At a July 9 planning board session, resident John Romano questioned how Hexa's application advanced and raised concerns about potential noise and pollution impacts on his property.
A case management conference was held in the Hexa Builders LLC and 3043 Williamstown Urban Renewal LLC v. Monroe Township case (Docket No. GLO-L-805-26).
Township Solicitor Sandra Graise stated the municipality is committed to vigorously and zealously defending the lawsuit while protecting residents' interests.

On July 28 Monroe attorney Todd Gelfand filed a four-page letter seeking dismissal, arguing the ban does not regulate the content of speech, a speaker, a message, or the plaintiffs' ability to engage in expressive activity.
Hexa Builders sued Monroe Township for more than $300 million in damages over the ban and the completeness review.
On August 1 Hexa's attorney Jim Maley asked the federal judge to reject Monroe Township's request to dismiss the lawsuit.
Hexa attorney Jim Maley filed a letter requesting remand of the non-constitutional state-law claims back to New Jersey Superior Court, arguing state courts have more expertise on local land use laws.

projects.name: Project Taurus (Raeden)
projects.note: Retrofit of an existing building on Garden of the Gods Road into the city's first AI data center, by California-based Raeden. Administratively approved by city staff in June 2026; the planning commission denied residents' appeals after a marathon hearing; two new appeals now send it to City Council, whose hearing must fall between Aug 29 and Sept 28 (likely mid-September - date not yet set). Chelsea Glen neighbors cite power, water, and noise from a prior Bitcoin operation at the site.

events.summary: KKTV reported that Oakland, California-based Raeden proposed 'Project Taurus,' a roughly 50-megawatt data center to replace a former Intel manufacturing plant near Garden of the Gods, and that a neighborhood meeting to hear resident concerns was scheduled for April 7, 2026, at the Hyatt Place hotel.
City planning department administratively approved the Project Taurus application in June 2026; neighbors immediately announced an appeal.

KRDO reported the city Planning Department administratively approved the Development Plan Modification on June 11, 2026, for the 21.96-acre former Intel site at 1565 High Tech Way, with residents given until 5 p.m. on June 22 to file appeals.

KRDO reported Raeden COO Jason Green said the company made voluntary modifications including generator relocation, enhanced noise monitoring, a $1 million bond, and third-party post-construction audits, while Integrity Matters' Dana Duggan criticized that residents were not notified until a day after the June 11 approval.

Per Integrity Matters, a citizen petition requesting a moratorium on data center approvals had gathered 5,349 signatures as of June 22, 2026, and a coalition of 33 appellants led by Katherine Kent and Ron Graham-Becker filed a formal appeal (City File No. DEPN-26-0039) challenging the Project Taurus approval.
Five appeals - including one from Chelsea Glen residents and the transparency group Integrity Matters - met the city's requirements to proceed.
Planning Commission denied the citizens' appeals after a ~14-hour hearing, upholding the approval 6-2.
Two new appeals filed, sending the decision to City Council - the final local authority. Hearing must occur between Aug 29 and Sept 28, 2026.

KRDO reported the Colorado Springs City Council announced its special meeting to hear the Project Taurus appeal would be held September 17, 2026, at 9 a.m. at the Pikes Peak Center for the Performing Arts, with up to 120 speakers allowed two minutes each.

projects.name: Deep Green downtown data center
projects.note: 24 MW data center plus a 16 MW fuel-cell plant on 2.5 acres near the Grand River downtown, with a closed-loop water-glycol cooling system (~500,000 gal/yr). The Planning Commission recommended the rezoning 5-2 in March 2026, but Deep Green withdrew its rezoning request on April 6, 2026, ending the proposal before a council vote.

events.summary: Lansing City Planning Commission voted 5-2 to recommend the rezoning for the 24 MW data center + 16 MW fuel-cell plant.
Deep Green withdrew its rezoning application, axing the downtown proposal before City Council voted.

projects.name: Stargate Abilene
projects.note: The flagship Stargate site, built by Crusoe on Lancium's Clean Campus - the most complete Stargate location, with roughly four of eight buildings operational (~0.3 GW live) as of mid-2026. OpenAI and Oracle capped the site at 1.2 GW in March 2026, dropping further expansion amid grid-interconnection delays exceeding a year. Power is a mix of on-site natural gas and grid supply.

events.summary: Taylor County Commissioners approved a Chapter 312 tax abatement for Lancium's $2.4 billion 'Project Artemis' data center campus, the largest project in Abilene/Taylor County history, starting at 200 MW with a goal to expand to 1 GW.

Crusoe and Lancium announced a partnership to build an initial 200 MW AI data center at the Lancium Clean Campus near Abilene, with plans to expand to 1.2 GW; two buildings totaling 980,000 square feet were expected to be energized in 2025.

The Development Corporation of Abilene, City of Abilene and Taylor County announced Crusoe's 998,000-square-foot data center at Lancium's Clean Campus, a combined estimated $3.4 billion investment on about 90 leased acres, to be leased to a Fortune 100 tenant in 2025.

At the White House on January 21, 2025, Trump announced the Stargate joint venture (OpenAI, Oracle, SoftBank) with up to $500 billion in AI infrastructure investment; Time reported construction had already begun on the Abilene, Texas data center that will house part of Stargate.

The Abilene City Council held a public hearing on a second 20-year tax abatement for Lancium covering 940.89 acres, abating 85% of tax liability while retaining 15%, projected to return $70-90 million to Abilene taxpayers over the term.

Taylor County residents raised concerns at a commissioners meeting about Lancium's tax breaks, citing energy viability, environmental hazards from heavy metals, and questioning whether Lancium should be classified as a data center rather than an energy grid; the final agreement vote was set for February 25.
The Abilene City Council voted to approve the amended tax abatement agreement for Lancium, with Mayor Weldon Hurt stating the data center would use less than 1% of Abilene's daily water consumption.

Crusoe announced it had begun second-phase construction at the Lancium Clean Campus, expanding the Abilene site to eight buildings, about 4 million square feet and 1.2 gigawatts, targeting completion by mid-2026.

Crusoe secured 4.5 GW of natural gas power through a joint venture with Engine No. 1, including seven GE Vernova turbines acquired by Engine No. 1 and Chevron to generate behind-the-meter power for AI data centers including Abilene.

Crusoe, Blue Owl Capital and Primary Digital Infrastructure announced the second phase of a $15 billion joint venture to fund the 1.2 GW Abilene campus, jointly sponsoring construction of six new buildings; a JPMorgan-led consortium provided a $7.1 billion construction loan.
As of July 2025, Oracle was contesting Taylor County's roughly $200 million appraised valuation of the first phase of the Abilene data center, despite already holding an 85% property tax abatement.

OpenAI and partners announced five new Stargate data center sites (including in Milam and Shackelford counties, Texas), with the Abilene flagship campus described as already running and delivering NVIDIA GB200 racks, as part of a pipeline totaling nearly 7 GW.
Crusoe announced the first phase of the Abilene campus is live and running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, with Oracle having begun delivering NVIDIA GB200 racks in June 2025.

Crusoe topped out the eighth and final building at the Abilene Stargate campus, acknowledging 7,000 tradespeople who contributed; the full campus encompasses approximately 4 million square feet with 1.2 GW total power capacity.

Crusoe's Abilene AI data center won 'North American Data Center Project of the Year' at the 2025 DCD Global Awards, cited for rapid 12-month modular delivery and direct-to-chip liquid cooling at 1.2 GW scale.

Texas Standard reported the $3.5 billion Stargate campus had about 6,000 construction workers on site, received an 85% property tax abatement over 10 years, and was expected to create roughly 300 permanent jobs upon completion.

Time reported Abilene's average monthly rent had risen to $2,395 (up about $1,000 year-over-year), the Abilene Housing Authority documented a pre-existing deficit of approximately 5,600 housing units exacerbated by the Stargate worker influx, and voucher placement rates had dropped from 80% to about 50%.
In March 2026 OpenAI and Oracle capped the Abilene site at 1.2 GW, dropping expansion plans amid grid delays of more than a year; later buildings have run behind their permitted schedules.

KTXS reported Lancium and Crusoe executives briefed Abilene city leaders that construction on the roughly 4-million-square-foot, eight-building campus will run through the first quarter of 2027, with about 9,000 craft workers on site daily and a closed-loop liquid-cooling design.

Crusoe announced a new 900 MW AI factory campus adjacent to the existing Abilene site to support Microsoft, with two buildings (each 336 MW critical IT) and a 900 MW on-site power plant, bringing total projected Abilene capacity to 2.1 GW; site prep was already underway with the first building expected energized mid-2027.
Speaking to the Kiwanis Club of Abilene, Lancium CEO Michael McNamara said the site is fully financed long-term, citing a 15-year Oracle lease and a 20-year Microsoft lease, per KTXS.

Local outlet KEYJ reported that Abilene residents launched a 'Save Abilene' website to organize opposition, citing concerns about housing costs, infrastructure strain, water usage, electric demand, and tax incentives relative to community benefits.

Distilled Earth reported that Crusoe's third and fourth Abilene buildings, begun in March 2025 and permitted for completion by March 2026, were still not online as of June 2026; Crusoe's CEO disclosed costs of $19.2 billion per GW including gas plants, and the site experienced multi-day winter outages from power and cooling equipment failures.

KUT/Texas Public Radio reported the Stargate build has driven an Abilene housing crisis, with average monthly rents near $2,600 (up roughly 50% year over year), about 9,000 construction workers on site, and about 1,000 permanent jobs expected once operational.

projects.name: EdgeCore Shannon Hill campus
projects.note: 697 acres purchased in the Shannon Hill Regional Business Park for a 3.9M sq ft, 1.1+ GW campus - a $17B+ investment announced June 2025, phased over several years. No construction start date or tenants disclosed at announcement. Part of a data-center surge in a small county that already hosts an AWS campus.

events.summary: Louisa County completed its purchase of 684 acres at the Shannon Hill exit off I-64 for $2.6 million to establish the Shannon Hill Regional Business Park, as reported in March 2019.
Virginia awarded Louisa County $300,000 through the Virginia Business Ready Sites Program for site readiness at the Shannon Hill Regional Business Park.
Louisa County received an $11.5 million state grant to bring water infrastructure to the 700-acre Shannon Hill Regional Business Park, the third-largest such grant awarded by the state.
EdgeCore announced the land purchase (697 ac, Shannon Hill Regional Business Park) and $17B+ phased campus plan in June 2025; construction timing and tenants undisclosed.

EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure announced the purchase of 697 acres at Shannon Hill Regional Business Park for $42 million and plans for a 1.1+ GW, 3.9 million sq ft data center campus with $17 billion total investment.
Governor Youngkin praised the EdgeCore deal; a spokesperson confirmed the commonwealth provided no state incentives, though Virginia had previously awarded $300,000 in site-readiness funds in 2022.

Bisnow reported Louisa County had invested approximately $29.5 million in utilities infrastructure at Shannon Hill using $13.6 million in grants and $17 million in debt, with the county purchasing the land in 2018 for $2.6 million and rezoning it in 2019 for technology uses.

CBS19 reported EdgeCore plans a closed-loop air-cooled system with minimal water usage and significant landscape buffers; Rappahannock Electric Cooperative and its affiliate Hyperscale Energy Services will provide power.

Information Charlottesville reported the Shannon Hill sale closed for $42 million; IDA Chairman Dustin Madison stated the announcement marks a realization of the park's full benefits; proceeds will pay down county debt early.

Local newsletter reported that EdgeCore's Shannon Hill campus will draw water from the James River via a pipeline expected mid-2026, not from the local Northeast Creek Reservoir, differentiating it from the concurrent AWS proposal.

Louisa County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a performance agreement with EdgeCore providing annual performance grants of 15% of real and business personal property tax revenue, capped at $15 million total, with payments from 2027 through 2041.

GovTech reported Louisa County sold Shannon Hill to EdgeCore and proceeded with the project despite resident concerns, contrasting it with Amazon's separate withdrawal under stronger community opposition.

EdgeCore reported entering 2026 with 1.8 GW of capacity delivered or under development across six markets including Louisa County, with $5.9 billion in equity and debt committed and $16.1 billion planned for future development.

Louisa County Supervisor Manning Woodward stated EdgeCore will operate behind-the-meter power generation at Shannon Hill rather than drawing from the grid; gas-fired generation is the near-term option, with small modular reactors described as far off.

U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Norfolk District published public notice NAO-2025-00089 / MRC-2026-1381 for EdgeCore Louisa Phase 2, proposing fill of 4.20 acres of wetlands and 6,302 linear feet of stream for three data center buildings and substations on 187 acres, filed via EDI Louisa 1, LLC.

projects.name: Google West Texas campuses
projects.note: Part of Google's $40B Texas investment through 2027: AI data-center campuses in Haskell County (one paired with a new Intersect/TPG solar + battery storage plant) and Armstrong County, plus additional sites in Pampa and Wilbarger Counties. Company-owned and proceeding, not a contested local rezoning.

events.summary: Intersect Power announced a strategic partnership with Google and TPG Rise Climate, backed by over $800 million in funding, to co-locate data centers with clean energy generation, with the first project (later identified as Quantum in Haskell County) expected operational in 2026.
Crusoe Energy began construction in May 2025 on Google's Armstrong County data center campus on 1,300 acres near Claude, Texas, according to Armstrong County Judge Adam Ensey.

KTXS reported that Google had purchased multiple properties near Lake Stamford for a data center, and that three new RV parks had been built in the past year to house workers, though Google had not yet formally announced the project.
Google announced a $40B Texas investment through 2027, including AI data-center hubs in Haskell and Armstrong Counties.

Governor Abbott and Google CEO Sundar Pichai announced Google's $40 billion Texas investment at an event in Midlothian, calling it Google's largest investment in any U.S. state, with three new data center campuses in Haskell and Armstrong Counties.

ABC7 Amarillo reported that Google's Armstrong County data center is being built by Crusoe Energy on 1,300 acres near Claude, TX, with construction underway since May 2025, 80-100 jobs expected, and completion targeted for late 2028 or early 2029.

Haskell County leaders gave mixed reactions to Google's plan: Mayor Isbell welcomed economic growth, while County Judge Thompson acknowledged concerns about agricultural land conversion but said renewable energy resources drove Google's site selection.

NewsChannel 6 reported that Haskell County's tax base of $800 million was expected to more than double from the Google data centers, with County Judge Kenny Thompson and Mayor Christina Isbell citing growth potential for the 3,000-person town.

Google held a two-hour community open house at the Museum of the West Texas Frontier in Stamford, fielding questions on water, roads, housing, and environmental impacts of its two Haskell County data centers.
Google announced a new air-cooled data center in Wilbarger County, Texas, co-located with AES clean energy generation under 20-year PPAs, as part of its broader West Texas expansion.

Stamford Mayor James Decker said the city is experiencing its first simultaneous multi-house construction since the 1980s, with rezoning for triplexes and revenue directed to street, water, sewer, and park improvements.
The Quantum Clean Energy Project (640 MW solar, 1.3 GWh battery storage) in Haskell County began operations in June 2026, co-located with a Google data center campus.

Google and Intersect announced the Meitner Energy Center in Gray and Roberts Counties, a 1 GW-plus co-located data center and wind/solar/battery generation complex, with construction running through December 2027.
Construction began on the Journey 2A data center building (210,420 sq ft) at the Haskell County 'Journey' campus, with a target completion in late October 2026.

projects.name: Augusta Township data center (Thor Equities)
projects.note: The township board rezoned 500+ acres of farmland near Milan from agricultural to general industrial for a hyperscale data center by NY-based Thor Equities. Residents petitioned the decision onto the ballot and voters overturned the rezoning 89.5%-10.4% on Aug 4, 2026 — a rare referendum defeat of an already-approved data-center rezoning.

events.summary: Voters overturned the industrial rezoning 89.5% to 10.4%, blocking the Thor Equities data center.

projects.name: Astra data center campus (Digital Realty)
projects.note: Digital Realty bought ~1,435 acres in the Astra Enterprise Park (the former Sunflower Army Ammunition Plant) to develop a ~600 MW campus across Astra North and South; first phase ~$4B excluding equipment, customer undisclosed. The second major data center proposed near the $4B Panasonic battery plant.

events.summary: Digital Realty's operating partnership closed the acquisition of approximately 1,440 acres at Astra Enterprise Park in De Soto for approximately $475 million in cash and operating partnership units, as disclosed in the company's June 22 press release.

Digital Realty presented preliminary plans for the Astra North data center campus to the De Soto City Council, describing nine buildings on 280 acres requiring 600 MW of power and up to 1 million gallons of water per day.

Ingram's reported Digital Realty unveiled plans for a $4 billion data center campus at Astra Enterprise Park in De Soto with 600 MW capacity across nine buildings, noting the land was purchased in April 2026 from Sunflower Redevelopment.
Digital Realty unveiled preliminary plans for a ~600 MW, ~1,435-acre campus at Astra Enterprise Park near the Panasonic battery plant.

Digital Realty officially announced the Astra Enterprise Park acquisition in an investor press release, disclosing the $475 million price, the Evergy Energy Service Agreement for 600 MW by early 2028 scalable to 2 GW, and that planning and phased development is underway.

KCUR reported De Soto Mayor Rick Walker welcomed data center growth as an opportunity to fund city functions, while resident Toni Caldwell raised concerns about lack of environmental impact studies and rapid development pace.

Commercial Property Executive reported Digital Realty entered the Kansas City market with its $475 million acquisition of 1,440 acres at Astra Enterprise Park, noting it secured an Evergy energy service agreement for 600 MW by early 2028.

Johnson County Post reported the Digital Realty campus would be De Soto's second data center, that the land is already zoned for data centers so no public hearing is required for site plan review, and that Digital Realty committed to fund over $300 million in power transmission upgrades.

The New Lede reported on De Soto residents organizing against data center development, including a national Facebook group 'Say NO to data centers' with 175,000 members run by De Soto-based resident Dally Holloway.

Digital Realty held a community information session from 5-7 pm at DYM Event Space in De Soto; residents attended with questions about water usage, noise, and the approval process, and some noted the company was more transparent than other Kansas data center developers.
On its Q2 2026 earnings call, Digital Realty referenced its expansion into the Kansas City metro with 600 MW of utility power beginning to ramp in early 2028 and a long-term runway of up to 2 GW.
Digital Realty submitted a site plan application for the Astra North campus to De Soto, with the Planning Commission expected to review it in August 2026; city staff review is underway.

projects.name: Posey County data center (Boberg/Hoenert Roads)
projects.locality: Posey County (Boberg & Hoenert Roads, near Mount Vernon)
projects.note: Commissioners stated at an Aug 4, 2026 meeting in Mount Vernon that they will vote no on the proposed data center near Boberg and Hoenert Roads, while continuing to evaluate proposals elsewhere in the county. The developer is unnamed; commissioners disclosed they signed an NDA despite no official proposal. Residents submitted hundreds of opposition letters and requested a two-year moratorium; no formal vote has been reported.

events.summary: Commissioners met at Hovey House in Mount Vernon; residents packed the room and delivered hundreds of opposition letters. Commissioners said they will vote no on the Boberg/Hoenert Roads data center but are still looking at proposals in other areas.

projects.name: Project Zora
projects.note: Developer controls roughly 1,200 acres of reclaimed mine land in northern Warrick County; the preliminary concept would develop about 300 acres and leave 900 as buffer. County officials met the Project Zora development team on July 30, 2026, emphasizing no votes, commitments, or NDAs were signed and that the developer's capacity/cost claims are unverified. The end user is expected to be publicly identified by end of 2026, with no permit applications before January 2027; commissioners held an Aug 11, 2026 special meeting on data-center zoning-code amendments.

events.summary: Warrick County officials and Economic Development representatives met with the Project Zora development team; no votes, commitments, or NDAs signed. Developer described control of ~1,200 acres of reclaimed mine land with ~300 acres proposed for development.

projects.name: AWS Northern Indiana expansion (New Carlisle)
projects.note: Amazon plans a $15B investment in new Northern Indiana data center campuses, additional to the $11B investment announced the prior year in St. Joseph County, where its New Carlisle data center already operates. Amazon secures 2.4 GW for its needs (3 GW total new grid capacity) and, through NIPSCO Generation LLC arrangements, will pay to use existing power lines and cover new power plant costs. Amazon says the expansion creates 1,100+ direct high-skilled jobs.

events.summary: Amazon announced a $15B plan for new Northern Indiana data center campuses on top of the earlier $11B St. Joseph County investment, with 2.4 GW of power secured via a NIPSCO cost-coverage arrangement. (Amazon's page carries no publication date; the announcement date is not asserted here.)

St. Joseph County approved a development facilitation agreement with shell company Razor5 LLC to evaluate 840 acres of farmland near New Carlisle for light-industrial use; Razor5 deposited $1 million in escrow for survey rights.

St. Joseph County Plan Commission recommended rezoning 640 acres south of the Indiana Enterprise Center from agricultural to industrial for the Razor5 project; a county council vote was scheduled for the following week.

Razor5 LLC presented preliminary plans to the St. Joseph County Council showing a potential total project investment of approximately $11 billion and filed a real property tax abatement application; the company behind Razor5 had not yet been publicly identified.

Governor Holcomb announced that Amazon Web Services would invest $11 billion to build a data center campus at the Indiana Enterprise Center near New Carlisle, creating at least 1,000 jobs — the largest capital investment in Indiana history.

St. Joseph County Council voted 7-2 to approve a 10-year 50% property tax abatement and a 35-year enterprise technology exemption (85% on data center equipment) for Amazon; the package included a $143 million community enhancement agreement for parks, schools, fire departments, and infrastructure.

AWS held a ceremonial groundbreaking at the Century Center in South Bend for its $11 billion data center campus on 870 acres near New Carlisle; construction was already underway, with the first four of 16 planned buildings targeted for completion by end of 2024.

More than 100 people attended an IDEM public hearing in New Carlisle on Amazon's Section 401 water quality certification application to fill approximately 10 acres of wetlands and reroute streams in the Kankakee River watershed; the Hoosier Environmental Council argued the proposed mitigation was insufficient.

IDEM cited Amazon for impacting nearly one acre of wetlands without authorization at the New Carlisle campus, ordered construction in state waters to cease, and required Amazon to withdraw its January 2025 permit application and resubmit with an additional 30% mitigation requirement.

Amazon announced plans to resubmit its IDEM wetland permit application after acknowledging its contractor Walbridge had impacted wetlands without authorization in late summer 2024; Amazon had not notified IDEM of the incident until May 2025.

The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved NiSource's petition to create NIPSCO Generation LLC (GenCo), a first-in-the-nation subsidiary utility to own, build, and manage generation assets exclusively for data centers in Northern Indiana, shielding existing NIPSCO retail customers from related costs.

Amazon announced that Project Rainier, its $11 billion data center campus in New Carlisle dedicated to training Anthropic's Claude AI models on approximately 500,000 Trainium2 chips, was now operational; CNBC reported it as the company's biggest AI data center.

Amazon announced an additional $15 billion investment to build new data center campuses in Northern Indiana, adding up to 3 GW of capacity; NIPSCO would supply power under a 15-year contract beginning January 2027, with GenCo planning two 1.3 GW gas plants and 400 MW of battery storage.

Four Republican St. Joseph County Council members sent a letter to Amazon requesting voluntary contributions toward homeowner property tax relief, noting AWS had nearly $38 million in abated property taxes in the first half of 2026 alone.

Indiana Citizen reported that the New Carlisle campus had 935 full-time employees as of December 2025 (average $40.99/hour), with construction traffic more than doubling the town's population daily at peak; Amazon requested permanent filling of over 9 acres of wetlands and rerouting of 5,000 feet of streams.

WNDU reported that AWS investment in the St. Joseph County campus had surpassed $13.8 billion, with approximately 18 of 30 planned buildings operational and over 1,000 people hired; a planned diverging diamond interchange at SR 2 and Larrison Boulevard had not yet begun construction.

projects.name: Project Flex
projects.note: Verrus (with Walbridge as general contractor) is developing the Project Flex data center on Milford Road in Lyon Township. The Planning Commission gave initial approval on Sept 8, 2025; final site-plan approval review is anticipated at the commission's Aug 24, 2026 meeting. Verrus is offering a $10M community benefits package and its attorney has warned of legal action if approval is further delayed; residents organized as 'No Data Center Lyon Township' oppose the project.

events.summary: Walbridge submitted the Project Flex site plan application to Lyon Township planning authorities for the 1.8-million-square-foot, 172-acre data center campus.
Lyon Township Planning Commission gave initial approval to Project Flex.

In December 2025 a Facebook opposition group titled 'NO DATA CENTER in Lyon Township' grew to roughly 2,000 members, citing concerns about electricity infrastructure, water usage, and environmental impacts.
Lyon Township issued an official press release/statement addressing questions about the Project Flex data center site plan.
Consulting firm Kimley-Horn completed a noise study for Project Flex, a condition of the site-plan approval.

Lyon Township issued a statement indicating the Planning Commission may be revisiting the conditional site-plan approval, saying final approval depends on independent review of the sound study and energy audit.
About 125 residents attended a Lyon Township Planning Commission meeting to voice opposition to the 1.8-million-square-foot data center.
Lyon Township held a study/informational meeting on the Project Flex data center; residents staged a protest outside before the meeting.
The Lyon Township Board of Trustees enacted a six-month moratorium on new data centers and facilities over 100,000 square feet, running through September 8, 2026, while it reviews ordinances.
The Oakland County Election Commission approved recall petition language targeting all seven Lyon Township trustees, an effort organizers tied to opposition to Project Flex.
An attorney for Verrus submitted a Final Site Plan response letter arguing the project meets township codes and warning of legal action if approval is further delayed.
At a Lyon Township Planning Commission meeting, dozens of residents, including State Sen. Jim Runestad, spoke during public comment opposing Project Flex.
In July 2026 Lyon Township postponed a decision on the data center, including whether to accept a $10 million community-benefits offer from Verrus.
Final approval review anticipated at the Lyon Township Planning Commission meeting.

projects.name: TeraWulf Cayuga data center (former Cayuga Power Plant)
projects.note: TeraWulf leases 183 acres of the 434-acre former Cayuga Power Plant site on Cayuga Lake in Lansing, NY, proposing ~125 acres of development: Phase 1 of 150 MW across three buildings plus a Phase 2 of another 150 MW. On April 27, 2026 the Lansing Planning Board deemed the site-plan application incomplete and requested lease details, construction-traffic data, and landscaping clarification; environmental groups' lawsuit over the Zoning Board's permit interpretation survived a standing challenge on April 29.

events.summary: Concurrent with the August 14, 2025 lease announcement, TeraWulf reported securing a multi-billion-dollar investment from Google tied to its expansion, with the Lansing site projecting about $400 million in redevelopment investment, roughly 500 temporary construction jobs, and 100 permanent positions.

On September 22, 2025 the Lansing Town Board held a public hearing on a proposed year-long development moratorium that would have paused major construction while the town rewrote its zoning laws; the final vote was deferred to a later meeting.
On November 5, 2025 the Lansing Town Board voted 3-2 not to withdraw its proposed construction moratorium, before reversing course later that month.

As reported November 14, 2025, a letter from TeraWulf's representatives called for withdrawal of the proposed moratorium and demanded the immediate resignation of Town Supervisor Ruth Groff and board member Joseph Wetmore, alleging Open Meetings Law, FOIL, and Lobbying Act violations.

On November 19, 2025 the Lansing Town Board unanimously voted to withdraw its proposed one-year land-use moratorium, without discussion or explanation, clearing a path for the TeraWulf project to advance.

On December 22, 2025 the Town of Lansing Zoning Board of Appeals voted 3-2 to classify TeraWulf's Cayuga site as 'general processing,' allowing the data center to proceed without additional rezoning or variances; it was the company's third appeal after prior rejections of 'scientific research laboratory' and 'warehouse' classifications.

On January 30, 2026, Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Now (CLEAN) and FLX Strong filed an Article 78 petition in New York State Supreme Court against the Lansing Zoning Board of Appeals and TeraWulf, seeking to annul the ZBA's December 2025 'general processing' classification as containing errors of law and procedural violations.
Lansing Planning Board reviewed TeraWulf's site-plan application, deemed it incomplete, and requested additional documentation (lease details, construction traffic data, landscaping clarification).
Court ruled that petitioners in the environmental groups' January lawsuit challenging the Zoning Board's permit interpretation have standing to proceed; arguments scheduled for June 18, 2026.

On June 17, 2026 a coalition of Finger Lakes organizations held a press event outside Lansing town hall to deliver the 'Reject the Development of an AI Data Center on Cayuga Lake' petition, which had gathered roughly 20,000 signatures (about 17,000 from New York State residents).
Opposition groups No Data Center FLX and FLX Strong hosted a public presentation on June 25, 2026 at the First Unitarian Society in Ithaca about data-center harms and the Lansing proposal.

As reported July 14, 2026, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed Executive Order No. 62 establishing a statewide moratorium halting state permitting for data centers of 50+ MW pending a Department of Public Service environmental review; the order exempts local-government permits, and TeraWulf said it does not change its Lansing plans.

projects.name: Dickerson Data Center Campus (Atmosphere)
projects.note: Atmosphere Data Centers (which took over the project from Terra Innovations, whose initial conditional-use application dates to January 2024) proposes a five-building data center campus on 110 acres at the decommissioned Dickerson Generating Station coal plant site; a major modification to the conditional use was filed in December 2025 and amended plans are on Montgomery Planning's development database. On 2026-07-28 the Montgomery County Council approved an 18-month moratorium on new data center approvals that encompasses this proposal; Office of Zoning and Administrative Appeals hearings had been scheduled for Sept 10-11, 2026.

events.summary: As reported December 4, 2025, the county hearing examiner had granted Terra Energy conditional use approval (case CU 24-13) for a data center complex at the Dickerson site, with the number and square footage of buildings left to future modifications.
A community forum on data centers was held in Rockville amid the debate over the Dickerson proposal, around the time County Executive Elrich first raised the possibility of a moratorium.

At a County Council hearing on data centers, approximately 30 speakers testified and 218 written testimonies were submitted; Atmosphere's proposal is described as a 300-megawatt campus on 110 acres seeking a Potomac River withdrawal cap of 500,000 gallons per day.
The Final Statement of Case and Operations in case CU 24-13(a)(A) for the Atmosphere Dickerson data center amendment is dated May 26, 2026, per the OZAH case record.
Atmosphere CEO Chuck McBride issued a statement saying the company respects the county's desire to take time to evaluate data center policies and appreciates the opportunity for public discussion.

County Executive Marc Elrich announced a six-month moratorium on data center permits by executive order at a Friday afternoon news conference, saying it creates time to establish clear rules before applications move through permitting.

County Executive Marc Elrich, at his weekly media briefing, acknowledged that Atmosphere Data Centers had filed an appeal of his data center moratorium with the county's Office of Zoning and Administrative Hearings.
Montgomery County Council approved an 18-month moratorium halting new data center approvals and applications, encompassing the Atmosphere proposal for a 110-acre, 5-building campus in Dickerson.
After the Council passed the 18-month moratorium, Atmosphere CEO Chuck McBride said the company was disappointed and would take time to fully evaluate the Council's action.
County Planning Board review of the project scheduled for July 30, 2026.
Office of Zoning and Administrative Appeals hearings on the conditional-use modification scheduled for Sept 10-11, 2026.

The Office of Zoning and Administrative Hearings lists the hearing on case CU 24-13(a)(A) (Atmosphere Dickerson Property Owner, LLC; conditional use holder Terra Energy, LLC) as scheduled for Thursday and Friday, November 12 and 13, 2026, at 9:30 a.m.

projects.name: Project Double Reed (Stream US Data Centers at STAMP)
projects.note: Stream US Data Centers proposes a $19.46 billion, three-building, roughly 600 MW data center campus at the STAMP site in the Town of Alabama, Genesee County. The Town Planning Board reviewed site-plan conditions (annual noise monitoring, heat-island mitigation, a dedicated code enforcement officer) and was expected to vote July 6, but both July meetings were cancelled after GCEDC, the SEQRA lead agency, could not complete environmental-review documentation; the next scheduled Planning Board meeting was Aug 3, 2026. GCEDC's CEO says the project keeps moving unless New York's passed-but-unsigned statewide data center moratorium becomes law.

events.summary: A GCEDC public hearing was held February 3, 2025 on the original Stream/Project Double Reed incentive proposal at STAMP, ahead of staff bringing a recommendation to the STAMP committee and full board.
The GCEDC Board of Directors approved the original 900,000-square-foot, 250-megawatt Project Double Reed data center plan for Stream U.S. Data Centers at STAMP on March 6, 2025.

The Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club filed suit in New York State Supreme Court alleging GCEDC violated SEQRA by awarding $472 million in subsidies to Stream U.S. Data Centers without conducting a full environmental review or requiring detailed project plans.

The GCEDC board voted to withdraw the State Environmental Quality Review determination for the approved 900,000-square-foot project after Stream said it had identified an opportunity to secure additional capacity and increase the project's scale, with Stream to submit an amended, larger application; a Tonawanda Seneca chief called the withdrawal a win.

Stream submitted a revised GCEDC SEQR application dated February 18, 2026 increasing the campus to a $19.46 billion, roughly 500 MW, 2.2 million-square-foot three-building project on about 90 acres, with roughly 125 permanent jobs.

At a March 31, 2026 meeting, a Wendel Companies engineer walked the Town of Alabama Planning Board through the Stream site plan (water, sanitary sewer, noise studies, generators, roads, emergency services, parking); the board made no decisions and scheduled a public hearing for April 20 at the Alabama Fire Department.

The Alabama Planning Board held a public hearing on the $19.46 billion Stream project at the Alabama Fire Hall with almost 75 speakers, a majority opposed over noise, water, wetlands and impacts near the Tonawanda Seneca Nation, while some trades union representatives supported it; Stream design manager Colm Curran presented the project.

On June 2, 2026, Wendel Companies engineers updated the Alabama Planning Board on draft site-plan conditions dated May 26, 2026 covering annual noise readings, construction traffic routes, a heat-island memorandum, stormwater, grading, utilities and safety; the board chair said there was no deadline for a decision.

Alabama Planning Board met for over 3.5 hours on the Stream site plan amid resident opposition; conditions discussed included lifetime annual noise monitoring and a one-year construction-start deadline, with a site-plan approval vote expected July 6.
Town supervisor announced the July 6 and July 20 Planning Board meetings were cancelled - GCEDC could not complete SEQRA documentation in time - with the next regular meeting set for Aug 3, 2026.

The Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club filed a lawsuit in New York State Supreme Court seeking to invalidate the zoning agreement between the Town of Alabama and the GCEDC that underpins development at the STAMP industrial park.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order on July 14, 2026 establishing New York's first statewide moratorium of up to one year, pausing the Department of Environmental Conservation from issuing discretionary environmental permits for new hyperscale data centers while the state builds a regulatory framework and Community Investment Framework.

On July 29, 2026 Governor Hochul held a roundtable in Henrietta defending the one-year data center moratorium she signed July 14, saying New York does not need to be first but wants to be the first to get it right and that developers should bear infrastructure costs; coverage tied the pause to Stream's proposed $19.5 billion STAMP campus in the Town of Alabama.

projects.name: Stonebridge Associates data center campus at Powder Mill Works
projects.note: Maryland-based Stonebridge Associates has applied to build a data center campus at the Powder Mill Works commercial development site spanning North Beaver and Mahoning townships in Lawrence County, PA. The application was rejected administratively because a required $3,000 Lawrence County escrow check was missing, and back-to-back zoning hearings in early August 2026 argued over whether the application was validly filed - which determines whether older April or newer June zoning rules apply. The zoning board deferred its ruling, expected within 45 days.

events.summary: Second zoning hearing (Mahoning Township) on whether Stonebridge's application was filed correctly and on time; the filing had been rejected over a missing $3,000 county escrow fee, and the board deferred its decision, indicating a ruling within 45 days.

projects.name: Prime Data Centers — Starpointe Business Park campus
projects.note: Prime Data Centers filed a conditional-use application in May 2026 for a seven-building, ~1.7 million sq ft data center campus with an attached behind-the-meter 450 MW gas-fired power plant on roughly 126 acres of reclaimed strip-mine land in the Starpointe Business Park (land owned by ALTIAN Development LLC), near the Pavilion at Starlake. The Aug. 5 conditional-use hearing drew 200+ residents; about three dozen won party status, and residents' attorneys argued the application belongs before the zoning hearing board rather than the supervisors, so the hearing was continued to Aug. 31 without Prime presenting.

events.summary: Prime Data Centers LLC filed a conditional-use application in May 2026 for a seven-building data center with an attached power generation facility in the Starpointe Business Park.
Hanover Township adopted an ordinance regulating data center development during a meeting in March 2026, before Prime Data Centers LLC submitted its Starpointe application.

CBS Pittsburgh reported that residents were mounting an 11th-hour fight against the proposed Starpointe data center ahead of the Aug. 5 hearing, citing health concerns from infrasound, noise and emissions and criticizing the township's data center ordinance as insufficiently protective on setbacks and noise.

Conditional-use hearing before Hanover Township supervisors drew hundreds of residents; roughly three dozen were granted party standing, and residents' attorneys argued the zoning hearing board must first determine the data center's comparable use, so the hearing was continued to Aug. 31.
Continued conditional-use hearing scheduled for 6 p.m. at the Hanover VFD Firehall.

projects.name: 900 Conshohocken Road data center (former Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill)
projects.note: 900 Conshohocken Road LLC, an entity of developer Brian O'Neill, seeks a special exception from Plymouth Township's zoning hearing board to convert the recently closed Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill — 10 existing buildings totaling about 2 million sq ft on 66 acres along the Schuylkill River — into a data center. The Aug. 6 hearing nearly filled a 750-seat auditorium; Conshohocken Borough was granted party status while Norristown was denied. The board set a procedural-only session for Aug. 17, with testimony continuing in September; an opposition petition has topped 4,000 signatures.

events.summary: The Plymouth Township Planning Agency voted 4-0 not to recommend a special exception to allow a data center at 900 Conshohocken Road.

A resident petition opposing the proposal had reached more than 400 signatures, led by Patricia Smith, citing environmental, proximity, and utility-cost concerns; the article noted the Cleveland-Cliffs mill was scheduled to close the following month.

A zoning hearing ended abruptly Monday night when the developer withdrew its application; the township solicitor said the applicant lacked legal standing because the agreement of sale had not been finalized.

Plymouth Township announced it had received a resubmitted zoning application from an entity tied to developer Brian O'Neill seeking a special exception for a data center in the Heavy Industrial district at 900 Conshohocken Road.

Plymouth Township Council issued a formal statement setting out its perspective on the proposed 900 Conshohocken Road data center and the zoning proceedings, and noted the public hearing set for June 25 at Colonial Middle School.

The zoning hearing kicked off at Colonial Middle School focused on procedural matters; party status was granted to Plymouth Township, the property owner's representatives, nearby residents, and the Borough of Conshohocken Authority, with no testimony taken.

Council Chair Lynne Viscio accused developer Brian O'Neill of bullying, saying the township would not be bullied or intimidated; O'Neill called the accusations a 'bold-faced lie,' and he challenged the validity of the township's zoning ordinance.

Zoning hearing board session at Colonial Middle School drew a nearly full 750-seat auditorium; the applicant's engineer began testimony comparing the data center to permitted heavy-industrial uses, and party-status requests from neighboring municipalities and residents were taken up.

At the Zoning Hearing Board session, residents booed and cursed as a witness testified data centers resemble manufacturing; the board rejected several legal motions filed by opponents and indicated it would continue the case in September.
Hearing continued to Aug. 17 for procedural matters only, with no witness testimony; further testimony to be scheduled.

projects.name: AWS Salem Township campus (Susquehanna nuclear plant)
projects.note: One of two initial sites in Amazon's announced $20B+ Pennsylvania data-center investment: a campus alongside the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station nuclear plant, where majority owner Talen Energy agreed to supply 960 MW. The original behind-the-meter connection drew FERC scrutiny and was blocked in 2024. The 960 MW figure is the contracted power supply, not built capacity.

events.summary: Talen Energy disclosed in an investor presentation that AWS acquired the 1,200-acre Cumulus data center campus co-located with the Susquehanna nuclear plant for $650 million ($350M at closing, $300M escrowed pending zoning milestones), with plans to develop up to 960 MW.

Salem Township supervisors voted to rezone approximately 1,582 acres into a new industrial Special Data Center Overlay District, enabling AWS to build up to 15 data center buildings; the township also agreed to a 10-year LERTA tax break at a 70 percent discount for Amazon.

PJM Interconnection filed with FERC for an amended interconnection service agreement to increase behind-the-meter power delivery from the Susquehanna nuclear plant to the co-located AWS data center from 300 MW to 480 MW.

American Electric Power and Exelon filed a protest with FERC challenging the amended ISA, arguing the co-location deal could shift up to $140 million in annual transmission costs onto other PJM ratepayers.
Talen Energy announced that the $300 million escrowed portion of the Cumulus campus purchase price was released after completion of zoning milestones allowing development of the AWS campus to 960 MW.

FERC voted 2-1 to reject the amended interconnection service agreement that would have increased behind-the-meter power from Susquehanna to the AWS data center from 300 MW to 480 MW, finding PJM failed to justify the departure from its standard agreement.
FERC issued an order deferring Talen Energy's November 20, 2024 rehearing request on the Susquehanna ISA rejection, stating it would address the request in a future order.

Talen Energy filed suit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit challenging FERC's November 2024 order rejecting the behind-the-meter interconnection agreement for the AWS data center at Susquehanna.

FERC upheld its rejection of the amended interconnection service agreement between PJM and Susquehanna Nuclear on rehearing, reaffirming its November 2024 order blocking expanded behind-the-meter power sales to the AWS data center.

Spotlight PA reported in June 2025 that Amazon's data centers qualify for Pennsylvania's sales tax exemption on data center equipment (enacted 2016, expanded 2021), with the state projecting $43 million in lost revenue for fiscal year 2025-26; critics noted no mandatory reporting of exempt transaction costs.

Amazon and Gov. Shapiro announced at least $20 billion for data center campuses in Pennsylvania, with initial sites in Salem Township (alongside the Susquehanna nuclear plant, with Talen Energy agreeing to provide 960 MW) and Falls Township, creating at least 1,250 permanent jobs.

Talen Energy and Amazon finalized a restructured 17-year, $18 billion power purchase agreement supplying up to 1,920 MW from Susquehanna via a grid-connected front-of-meter retail structure, bypassing the rejected behind-the-meter model; deliveries to ramp to 840-1,200 MW by 2029 and 1,680-1,920 MW by 2032.

FERC argued in an October 2025 brief to the Fifth Circuit that Talen's lawsuit should be dismissed as moot because the company had already contracted to abandon the behind-the-meter co-location arrangement at issue in the appeal.

QTS (owned by Blackstone) completed acquisition of approximately 1,700 acres from 96 Salem Township landowners for over $500 million, planning a 12-to-17 building data center campus adjacent to the AWS site using water-free cooling technology.

projects.name: AWS Falls Township campus (Keystone Trade Center)
projects.note: Second initial site of Amazon's $20B+ Pennsylvania investment: a data center at NorthPoint Development's Keystone Trade Center (1,800-acre former U.S. Steel Fairless Works site), including conversion of a planned 1M sq ft distribution building on a 247-acre parcel at 1 Ben Fairless Drive and a broader ~2M sq ft, 10-structure digital infrastructure campus. Falls Township supervisors approved revised preliminary/final land development plans for the data center use in March 2025.

events.summary: Falls Township announced Amazon will open a data center at the NorthPoint Development Keystone Trade Center site as part of Amazon's $20 billion Pennsylvania investment, with 1,250 jobs expected locally.

In March 2025, Falls Township supervisors approved revised preliminary and final land development plans converting the planned Building 6 distribution center at 1 Ben Fairless Drive to data center use.

projects.name: Social Circle data center complex (Fairplay Drive / Roy Malcom Road tracts)
projects.note: A data center complex assembled from three tracts totaling more than 450 acres on the southeast side of Fairplay Drive and Roy Malcom Road, from Social Circle Parkway to Hawkins Academy Road. The Social Circle Planning Commission voted unanimously at a called April 2026 meeting to recommend annexation, rezoning, special-use permitting and a future land use map change for the final 123-acre tract at 1402 Roy Malcom Road (concept plan: two buildings of about 248,600 sq ft each); the city council then approved all four requests 3-0 at a meeting reported May 1, 2026. Engineering firm Thomas & Hutton represents the property owner; project representatives say an unnamed 'end user' is already lined up and construction could begin in fall 2026.

events.summary: Council approved a special-use permit for a data center on a 181-acre tract along Fairplay Drive at Social Circle Parkway; councilmembers deadlocked 2-2 and Mayor David Keener broke the tie in favor. At the same meeting the council imposed a moratorium on new data center requests.
